record.title: A fair amount of slop: generative artificial intelligence and carelessness made cheap, unbounded and unattributable

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: In this paper the author argues that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has not created a new form of academic misconduct. Rather, it has taken the least-policed form of misconduct we had, that of cutting corners, and stripped it of the three properties that made it survivable. This 'sloppiness' was coupled to effort, bounded to one paper, and attributable to someone who lacked diligence. Fluent prose was once an 'honest signal', because it was costly to fake, and the apparatus of peer review built upon that cost. GenAI has broken that signal. Other things have broken too, including the evidence chain. 'Citation laundering' is where a fabricated claim, cited once by an author linking it to a real source, acquires a provenance despite it being unreachable by any reference check. The author highlights research in health professions education in which various authors have admitted to citing work they have not read, and argues that current GenAI use declarations are largely uncalibrated instruments. The closest look health professions education scholars seem to have taken at their own reference lists appears to predate these tools, and because syntheses inform guidelines and guidelines inform curricula, a fabricated claim can travel from a 'prompt' to what a clinician teaches at the bedside. Because journals' workflows have not traditionally involved verification, blame for abuses all too often falls on reviewers, who are ill equipped to carry it. Ultimately, the use of GenAI means that much of our cognitive effort needs to be relocated from the act of writing into a deliberate act of adjudication. The author describes how this paper was itself produced using GenAI to bring back effortful, bounded and attributable practice leading to a worked example of disclosure that describes practice rather than certifying intention.

record.title: AI-powered human action recognition of functional activities in stroke: a systematic review

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI)-based human activity recognition (HAR) is a promising approach for detecting functional activity in individuals with stroke, potentially enabling objective and ecologically valid assessment, monitoring and treatment. We aimed to synthesize current evidence on AI-based HAR for functional activity recognition after stroke, focusing on sensing technologies, target activities, settings, and model architectures. PubMed, Embase, WOS, and Scopus were searched and seventeen studies involving 224 individuals with stroke met the inclusion criteria. Inertial measurement units were the predominant sensing modality (12/17, 70.6%), with several studies demonstrating the feasibility of recognizing relevant functional activities using a single device. Single-sensor approaches were also used in home-based and simulated-home settings, suggesting potential for scalable and unobtrusive monitoring outside clinical environments; however, most studies were conducted in controlled clinical settings (11/17, 64.7%), with limited real-world validation to date. Convolutional neural networks were the most frequently used deep learning architecture, while Random Forest was the most common traditional machine learning method. Multimodal sensing may enrich activity characterization, although greater sensing complexity may reduce feasibility for prolonged home monitoring. Methodological and reporting limitations, including concerns regarding confounding and reproducibility, should be considered when interpreting the current evidence. Overall, single-sensor AI-based HAR appears promising for low-burden, continuous, and ecologically valid monitoring. Future research should prioritize longitudinal validation in everyday environments, transparent reporting of code and data availability, and inclusion of acute and severely impaired stroke populations to facilitate clinical translation toward objective monitoring, personalized rehabilitation, and remote care.

record.abstract_text: The increasing adoption of digital technologies and online learning platforms has transformed higher education, making digital literacy an important competency for media students. However, existing learning analytics approaches primarily focus on academic performance prediction while providing limited attention to digital-literacy-related behavioral patterns and the interpretability of predictive models. Furthermore, conventional machine learning techniques often fail to capture the temporal behavioural patterns generated through learner interactions within Learning Management Systems (LMSs). To address these challenges, this study proposes an Explainable BiLSTM-Attention Learning Analytics Framework for predicting MDLA-derived digital-literacy behavioral proxy categories using learner behavioural data extracted from the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD). Because OULAD does not contain independently measured digital-literacy scores, the Low, Medium, and High target categories are derived from LMS behavioral information through the proposed Media Digital Literacy Analytics (MDLA) representation and are treated as behavioral proxy categories rather than directly measured levels of digital literacy. The proposed framework combines a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with an attention mechanism to model sequential learner behaviour, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and attention visualization improve model transparency and interpretability. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework obtained higher scores than the evaluated baselines in a single run on OULAD, the evaluated machine learning and deep learning baseline models, achieving an Accuracy of 95.8%, Precision of 95.1%, Recall of 94.7%, F1-score of 94.9%, and a ROC-AUC of 97.2%. Explainability analysis identified engagement duration, assessment performance, resource usage, forum participation, and interaction frequency as the most influential behavioural factors contributing to the prediction of the MDLA-derived proxy categories. The findings suggest that integrating sequential deep learning with explainable learning analytics can model digital-literacy-related behavioral profiles in this OULAD setting. MDLA is a behavioral representation and has not been validated against a standardized digital-literacy assessment. The findings are based on a single dataset (OULAD) and a single experimental run, and should not be generalized to other institutions, LMS platforms, or learner populations without external validation. record.abstract_text: Abstract Despite its promise, adaptive learning faces significant technological, pedagogical, and infrastructural challenges that hinder its large-scale adoption. This study explores pedagogical obstacles from the perspectives of educators and instructional designers, focusing on their practices, perceptions, and specific needs. A mixed-methods approach combined a quantitative survey with qualitative data. Data were collected from 90 education professionals (teachers, instructional designers, and trainers) reached through LinkedIn and academic networks. Most participants (82.2%) identified situations requiring adaptation, yet only 55.6% had implemented adaptive measures. The qualitative analysis identified four main categories of adaptation practices. Participants expressed strong interest in AI-powered features to support instructional design tasks. The study proposes actionable recommendations to bridge the gap between technology and pedagogy, including the use of AI-assisted tools combined with human expertise, the development of adaptive interactive content and investment in professional development. This balanced approach aims to address critical barriers while maintaining educational quality and effectiveness, contributing to a better understanding of how AI can be integrated into adaptive learning systems to address current challenges.

record.title: Generative artificial intelligence usage by university students in the light of Diffusion of Innovations theory

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, has fundamentally transformed the landscape of higher education. This study investigates the factors influencing the adoption of generative AI by university students through the theoretical lens of Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory. Drawing upon Rogers’ seminal framework, this research examines how five perceived attributes of innovation-relative advantage, compatibility, simplicity, trialability, and observability-is related to students’ behavioral intention to use generative AI tools in their academic pursuits. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among students from multiple Polish universities, and the collected data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties, with all constructs achieving acceptable levels of internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The structural model results indicate that relative advantage, simplicity, observability and compatibility are significantly related to behavioral intention, while trialability demonstrates a non-significant effect. The model explains approximately 48.7% of variance in behavioral intention. These findings contribute to the theoretical understanding of technology adoption in educational contexts and provide practical implications for higher education institutions seeking to integrate generative AI tools into their pedagogical frameworks. The study concludes with recommendations for fostering responsible AI adoption while addressing concerns regarding academic integrity and critical thinking development.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: This study examines the relationship between prompt engineering literacy and academic learning outcomes among tertiary-level students in Bangladesh, with particular attention to the ethical dimensions of artificial intelligence (AI) integration in higher education. Using a concurrent mixed methods design, data were collected from students across public, private, and National University-affiliated institutions through online forms, telephone surveys, and messaging-platform surveys, complemented by key informant interviews with students and educators. The findings show that students with stronger prompt engineering knowledge achieved substantially larger gains on a post-intervention knowledge assessment, and that this knowledge, together with the frequency and perceived usefulness of AI engagement, was the strongest independent predictor of learning outcomes, ahead of institutional type. Ethical concerns, most notably academic dishonesty, algorithmic bias, and overreliance on automation, were widely recognized by students, yet formal institutional guidance on ethical AI use remained rare and was almost entirely absent among National University-affiliated colleges. These results carry direct implications for policy and practice. They suggest that prompt engineering merits treatment as a foundational academic literacy rather than a technical add-on, that AI ethics training needs to reach under-resourced institutions as a matter of priority, and that closing the gap between how quickly students adopt AI and how slowly institutions govern it is now an urgent task for Bangladeshi higher education.

record.title: Source transparency and accuracy warnings support more selective reliance on generative-AI answers in a randomized online experiment

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative-AI systems increasingly provide answers to everyday questions, but users need to decide not only whether to accept an answer, but whether acceptance should depend on answer correctness. This randomized online experiment tested whether visible source information and an accuracy warning supported more selective reliance on AI-style answers. A final analytic sample of 800 adult participants was assigned to one of four between-subjects cue conditions in a 2 × 2 × 2 mixed design crossing source transparency (absent vs. present), accuracy warning (absent vs. present), and answer correctness (incorrect vs. correct, within participant). Each participant evaluated 24 AI-style answers, yielding 19,200 trial-level observations. The primary analysis used all trials and modelled acceptance as a function of source transparency, accuracy warning, answer correctness, and their interactions. Participants accepted correct answers more often than incorrect answers, and the correct-incorrect acceptance gap was largest in the source-plus-warning condition. In the applied-risk model restricted to incorrect-answer trials, acceptance of incorrect answers was highest in the control condition (1080/2400, 45%) and lower in the source-only (864/2400, 36%), warning-only (672/2400, 28%), and source-plus-warning conditions (504/2400, 21%). Verification behaviour was highest in the combined condition (2496/4800, 52%). These results indicate that brief on-screen cues lowered erroneous-answer acceptance and encouraged verification in low-risk information-evaluation tasks, while the distinction between response bias and sensitivity remains an important boundary condition.

record.abstract_text: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption at work has documented heterogeneity in user attitudes and adoption profiles, but less is known about whether employees differ in how they weight adoption-relevant information. In a within-subject structured-profile experiment, 446 employees provided 7,136 intention judgments across 16 profiles that varied AI adoption benefits, barriers, replacement vulnerability, and anticipated work harm. Multilevel regression mixture model analysis identified four latent decision-policy classes with different estimated weights on opportunity and threat cues; class mean intentions were not statistically distinguishable. Drawing on multiple-cue judgment theory, we interpret this pattern as heterogeneity in cue utilization rather than simply in attitude levels. Explaining and managing AI adoption therefore requires attention to latent decision policies, because aggregate effect estimates and profiles based on mean levels can conceal differences in cue responsiveness that shape how employees evaluate AI.

record.title: Consent to passive sensing in artificial intelligence-personalized interfaces: perceived surveillance, transparency, and trust

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Artificial intelligence-personalized interfaces increasingly use passive behavioral signals generated during ordinary interaction. Such sensing can support personalization but may also heighten perceived surveillance and reduce users’ sense of control. Across two sequential experiments, we tested how data collection type (active sharing vs. passive sensing) and consent design quality (low vs. high transparency/control) shape privacy appraisals, trust, and consent. Study 1 (N = 855) showed that passive sensing increased perceived surveillance and creepiness and reduced trust, consent willingness, and behavioral acceptance, particularly under low transparency/control. High transparency/control increased perceived control and attenuated these effects. Study 2 replicated the principal self-report pattern in a laboratory setting and added eye tracking and galvanic skin response (GSR)/electrodermal activity. Passive sensing increased attention to data-use and decision-relevant elements and produced greater baseline-adjusted electrodermal arousal, with the clearest transparency/control buffering during the decision window. Process measures did not add explanatory value for trust or consent willingness, although an exploratory model indicated that GSR measures improved prediction of behavioral acceptance. Passive sensing should therefore be treated as a consent and privacy design issue, not only as a technical mechanism for personalization.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Objective Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes are rapidly becoming normalized in clinical practice, yet governance frameworks focus on accuracy, privacy, consent, and medicolegal status. Risks to clinician capabilities have received less attention. Speak before the reveal is a proposed method in which clinicians verbalize critical cognitive steps, such as synthesis and plan, before note generation. Discussion Recent work distinguishes deskilling in senior clinicians, never-skilling from premature offload in trainees and mis-skilling, the internalization of AI errors and inappropriate use as sound practice. This Perspective builds on emerging evidence that reasoning before seeing AI output may protect unaided reasoning. Training implementation, evaluation, adherence challenges, validation methodology, and governance strategies for training bodies, health services, and scribe vendors are discussed. Conclusion Speak before the reveal is a low-cost, testable approach to maintaining clinical reasoning for individuals or organizations. Successful AI scribe adoption requires preserving clinicians’ ability to work without AI support.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are one of the leading causes of maternal morbidity and mortality in Colombia, particularly in rural regions with limited access to specialized care. In this context, Preeclapp was developed as a clinical decision support system grounded in expert-system logic, designed to provide guideline-based support for maternal care in settings with limited resources and connectivity. This proof-of-concept implementation study analyzes the integration of Preeclapp into clinical practice and the factors that influenced its adoption. The main barriers identified included unstable connectivity, lack of data interoperability, high staff turnover, and initial skepticism toward AI-based technologies. Nevertheless, the project showed preliminary feasibility of use by non-specialized personnel in obstetrics and gynecology, even in low-connectivity environments. To overcome these challenges, the project relied on training sessions, embedded educational resources, continuous technical support, and iterative software adaptations. Our implementation suggests that these strategies were perceived by users as supporting adherence to obstetric protocols, reinforcing clinical decision-making, and enhancing staff confidence, particularly in facilities with limited specialist availability. As a proof-of-concept implementation study, this work did not evaluate diagnostic accuracy or clinical effectiveness; instead, it focused on early implementation feasibility, usability, acceptability, and perceived usefulness. The findings suggest that sustainable adoption of AI-CDSS systems requires strengthening digital literacy and promoting a culture of innovation. Our experience with Preeclapp indicates that adoption and implementation benefited from a modular design, low-connectivity functionality, flexibility, and co-creation with local teams, which helped adapt the tool to each institution’s context.

record.abstract_text: Abstract This article theorizes financial markets and democratic publics as collective information-processing systems embedded in shared communicative infrastructures, such that markets can even be said to be embedded in publics. Bringing the efficient market hypothesis into dialogue with the liberal marketplace of ideas and the Habermasian public sphere, I identify four epistemic conditions these traditions depend on: diversity, independence, aggregation, and correction. I argue that price discovery is epistemically embedded in the same media environment through which public opinions form. The attention economy of engagement-driven media brings this into view by degrading that environment: it privileges affective arousal over informational quality, correlates judgements, and suppresses correction, in effect creating corrupted marketplaces of ideas. The comparison also shows a specific difference between the domains: market correction through arbitrage operates through market transactions as well as media communication, whereas counterspeech and persuasion in publics are more reliant on media, arguably rendering publics more vulnerable to media impairment.

record.abstract_text: Purpose This study, guided by the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (CTML), investigates how multimodal large language models (MLLMs) mediate the professional learning of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pre-service teachers within Chinese lesson study (CLS). It aims to elucidate the cognitive and dialogic mechanisms through which AI-supported mediation shapes teacher learning processes and participation. Design/methodology/approach A three-month intervention integrating MLLMs into CLS was conducted with 50 EFL pre-service teachers at a Chinese normal university. Adopting an interpretive qualitative design, data were collected from longitudinal reflective journals, MLLM interaction logs, field notes and two rounds of semi-structured interviews with 5 purposively selected focal participants. Data analysis combined deductive coding based on CTML (intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load) with inductive thematic analysis to capture emergent patterns of AI-mediated learning and interaction. Findings The findings reveal that MLLMs functioned as cognitive-dialogic mediators in three key ways: (1) reducing linguistic and organizational barriers, thereby lowering extraneous cognitive load; (2) redistributing cognitive resources to support meaning-making and pedagogical reasoning; and (3) enabling deeper engagement in collaborative knowledge construction and reflective inquiry within CLS. However, participants also reported tensions related to epistemic reliability and the risk of overreliance on AI-generated outputs, indicating a shift in cognitive demands from knowledge construction to evaluation and regulation. Originality/value This study advances the field by proposing a cognitive-dialogic framework that brings CTML into dialog with sociocultural perspectives on mediation, offering a nuanced account of how AI reshapes teacher learning in practice-based settings. It contributes empirical evidence on the role of MLLMs as mediating tools in CLS and provides design implications for cognitively and ethically informed AI integration in teacher education.

record.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how algorithmic monitoring shapes gig workers’ psychological well-being through passive and active algorithmic resistance. It further investigates whether algorithmic fairness alters the relationship between algorithmic monitoring and resistance behaviors. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a two-study quantitative design. Study 1 applies a three-wave survey of 224 gig workers in Pakistan, with four-week intervals between each wave. Algorithmic monitoring and algorithmic fairness were measured at Time 1, passive and active algorithmic resistance at Time 2 and psychological well-being at Time 3. Study 2 uses a 2 × 2 experiment with 115 participants, manipulating algorithmic monitoring and algorithmic fairness and examining resistance responses and psychological well-being. Findings Study 1 shows that algorithmic monitoring is positively related to passive and active algorithmic resistance, and that both forms of resistance are negatively related to psychological well-being. Passive and active resistance also mediate the relationship between algorithmic monitoring and well-being. Algorithmic fairness weakens the relationship between monitoring and active resistance. Study 2 shows significant interactions between algorithmic monitoring and algorithmic fairness for passive resistance, active resistance and psychological well-being, although the observed resistance patterns differ from the hypothesized form. Originality/value This study advances algorithmic human resource management (HRM) research by showing that gig workers do not merely experience algorithmic monitoring passively but respond through distinct forms of resistance that have implications for psychological well-being. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative approach based on in-depth interviews with 32 knowledge workers who work directly with GenAI tools, combining inductive coding with abductive interpretation. Findings The findings identify authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. When GenAI contributes to ideation, analysis, drafting, coding or other knowledge-intensive outputs, workers may find it difficult to distinguish their own contribution from that of the technology. Participants responded to this ambiguity differently. Some reconstructed their expertise around judgment, validation and contextualization and experienced GenAI as extending their professional capability. Others struggled to internalize successful outputs as evidence of their own competence and reported impostor-like experiences and reduced meaningfulness. The findings suggest that experiences of GenAI-enabled co-production depend on whether workers interpret and reconstruct their contribution. Practical implications Managers in comparable knowledge-intensive settings may consider making human judgment visible, clarifying legitimate uses of GenAI and recognizing contributions beyond output speed and quality. Originality/value This study identifies authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. It shows how uncertainty regarding the respective contributions of the worker and GenAI can complicate competence attribution and initiate sensemaking about professional contribution. By explaining how workers' interpretations of authorship ambiguity are associated with divergent identity and meaning outcomes, including enhanced capability, impostor-like experiences and changing meaningfulness, the study extends research on human–AI collaboration beyond its predominant focus on performance and productivity.

Because the detection community rarely reports how much energy a particular detector uses, twenty YOLO object detection models were trained on 13,639 aerial and satellite images of illegal mining equipment from Colombia, in three categories, reporting both detection accuracy and the energy required on the same instrumentation. In previous work, a local large language model was used to find hyperparameter values based upon the training history of YOLOv8. Energy per image spanned a factor of 28, from 0.7 to 19.5 J, against a spread of only 0.14 mAP@50-95 in accuracy, so the detector was selected on marginal accuracy return per joule, at the knee of the Pareto front, rather than on accuracy alone. The knee where accuracy falls off occurred at YOLO26m, which produced 0.7260 mAP@50-95 on a previously unseen test dataset for 2048 mJ. Next, three of these models were compiled to INT8 for a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-8L accelerator, which served as a proxy for a nanosatellite payload. The workstation ranking did not survive compilation. There were changes at both ends: the model that ranked highest on the GPU lost 0.160 mAP@50-95 and finished last, while the two middle-ranked models switched positions. Both changes were confined to localization rather than recognition, and both fell on the head that regresses box coordinates directly. The attention-based model attempted (YOLO12m) could not be compiled for the accelerator.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: As generative AI reshapes professional and educational practice, institutions face a challenge: how to support diverse learners, from non-coders to advanced students, in building confidence and practice with AI-supported problem solving. Most institutional responses bifurcate into conceptual workshops for general audiences or technical courses for computer science majors, leaving few spaces where mixed-ability learners can engage common AI tasks at levels matched to their prior experience. This experience report presents the LearnAI Framework, a two-layer model for just-in-time AI co-creation piloted at a comprehensive teaching university. The Wide-Exposure Layer embeds short presentations in existing courses to build AI awareness at scale, reaching students and faculty across 18 courses in five disciplines. The Customized Co-Creation Layer provides opt-in, one-on-one sessions where clients work with trained undergraduate tutors through a 5-Stage Pedagogical Script: Problem Framing, Tool-Task Mapping, Iterative Co-Prompting, Deployment and Verification, and Ethical Reflection. Over two semesters, 35 clients co-created 36 portfolio websites and over 20 deployed web applications. Interviews with five clients and two tutors suggest a recurring change in how clients described AI use, shifting from treating AI as a passive answer machine to engaging it as a collaborative tool under human direction. A small paired pre/post AI readiness dataset (N=7) provides preliminary descriptive context, and tutor accounts document how the pedagogical script was enacted and adapted across client types. We report on boundary cases including clients who felt overwhelmed and respondents who deliberately rejected AI use. This paper contributes a practical, adoptable framework with initial evidence from a single institution.

record.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
record.abstract_text: Silicon Lifecycle Management (SLM) is essential for ensuring the reliability, security, and performance of modern computing platforms. Conventional SLM approaches rely on off-chip or software-only analytics, which lack on-die interpretability. We present X-OCTANE, an explainable on-chip telemetry-based anomaly notification engine. X–OCTANE is a hybrid explainability framework that integrates Causal-Preserving Mutual Information (CP–MI) with SHAP-based feature attribution for interpretable feature ranking and selection. The proposed feature rank-and-selection procedure retains competitive safety-oriented anomaly detection and bolsters security-specific in-field monitoring of compute platforms. For the 7 nm ASAP technology, X-OCTANE achieves competitive anomaly detection performance with less than 0.50% CPU die area and 1.0% non-idle power overhead. In addition, X–OCTANE improves anomaly-driven diagnosis accuracy by over 7% on average. Experimental validation using the PAMPAR benchmark suite on two separate experimental platforms demonstrates enhanced anomaly detection and diagnosis through the proposed explainable feature-rank-and-selection method. X–OCTANE establishes a scalable and transparent foundation for on-chip SLM analytics, unifying detection fidelity with causal interpretability.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
record.abstract_text: To address the growing computational demands of high-performance computing (HPC) and machine learning (ML) applications, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) have transitioned from single-chip designs to multi-chip module (MCM) architectures, driven by manufacturing constraints. Simultaneously, GPUs are increasingly deployed in cloud environments to accelerate a wide range of applications for multiple users. Spatial multitasking, which allows multiple applications to run concurrently on a single GPU by executing them on different sets of streaming multiprocessors (SMs), offers an efficient method for sharing GPU resources. However, effectively supporting multitasking in the emerging MCM-GPU architecture presents a significant challenge that remains an open problem. This article presents the key observation that the placement of co-executing applications in MCM-GPUs plays a critical role in system performance. Specifically, for certain multiprogram workloads, co-executing applications achieve better performance when located on the same GPU chip to maximize memory bandwidth utilization. Conversely, other workloads benefit from being distributed across different GPU chips to mitigate memory contention. To address this, we propose a Location-Aware Scheduler (LA-Scheduler) that identifies application characteristics and makes optimized scheduling decisions. The LA-Scheduler performs lightweight workload classification using a k-means-based clustering method and applies multitasking scheduling rules during runtime to determine the optimal placement of applications within the MCM-GPU architecture. Evaluation results show that the proposed LA-Scheduler improves system throughput (STP) by an average of 38.67% compared with single-task operation. Compared with the traditional methods intra-chip scheduling and inter-chip scheduling, the system throughput is improved by an average of 13.51% and 7.14% respectively.

record.abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) have great potential to enhance productivity in many disciplines, such as software engineering. However, it is unclear to what extent they can assist in the design process of electronic circuits. This article focuses on the application of LLMs to switched-mode power supply (SMPS) design for printed circuit boards (PCBs). We present multiple LLM-based workflows that combine reasoning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a custom toolkit that enables the LLM to interact with the SPICE circuit simulator to receive physical feedback. Two benchmark experiments are presented to analyze the performance of LLM-based assistants on various design tasks. These include parameter tuning and topology adaption, as well as design optimization of SMPS circuits through optimal catalogue component selection to maximize circuit efficiency or balance multiple objectives like size, ripple, and component loss. Experiment results show that SPICE simulation feedback and current LLM advancements, such as reasoning, significantly increase the solve rate on 269 manually created benchmark tasks from 15% to 91%. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that most parameter tuning design tasks can be solved, while limits remain for certain topology adaption and multi-objective optimization tasks. Our experiments offer insights for improving current concepts, for example by adapting text-based circuit representations.

record.title: Socrates went nuclear: Comparing Interaction Strategies for AI systems in a Learning Context using Brain Sensing

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Students are adopting LLMs at scale. This poses a question: does unrestricted AI access bypass the cognitive effort required for learning, or does it streamline knowledge acquisition? This paper reports on a study where we compare three designs for user-AI interaction in a learning context: (1) an unrestricted conversational bot like ChatGPT, (2) a pedagogically constrained bot that guides through hints without giving final answers, which we refer to as the Socratic mode; and (3) a non-conversational adaptive tutoring system that adjusts difficulty in real-time based on the user’s cognitive engagement derived from the brain signals. Fifty study participants were tasked with learning about nuclear safety protocols, a domain chosen for its zero-prior knowledge baseline. The participants progressed through an instructional video, a pre-test, an AI-driven assessment phase, which varied in the three conditions, and an immediate post-test. The nature of the questions centered primarily on factual knowledge acquisition, but it still required participants to have a global understanding of the concepts in order to answer the questions correctly. A Muse headband was used to derive the cognitive engagement of all users in all conditions. The unrestricted chatbot produced higher learning gains (delta) than both constrained modes ( p <.03, d > 0.80), while the adaptive condition generated significantly higher EEG engagement ( p =.018). The cluster analysis of chatbot usage and discussion patterns by users showed that most participants in the unrestricted-mode adopted a direct answer-retrieval strategy, while participants in the Socratic-mode initially attempted to reason through the hints before progressively disengaging. Consequently, this also suggests that the success of the unrestricted AI is not an evidence of deeper learning, but rather a result of the immediate post-test evaluation after the training phase.

record.abstract_text: Table Question Answering (TableQA) requires reasoning over natural language questions and structured tables and remains challenging due to noisy evidence and complex multi-step reasoning. Recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based approaches typically adopt decomposition–reasoning–validation pipelines that combine Chain-of-Thought (CoT) decomposition, Direct Prompting (DP), Python Agent (PyAgent) execution, and self-validation. However, these methods still largely rely on unconstrained LLM reasoning during decomposition, which may introduce unsupported sub-questions and irrelevant evidence expansion. We propose EV idence- A ware (EVA), a framework that explicitly grounds decomposition on question-relevant table evidence before reasoning begins. EVA first extracts evidence-aware relational structures that associate question semantics with supporting table attributes, thereby constraining sub-question generation within a grounded evidence space. EVA further introduces relation-guided validation and integrates both DP and PyAgent reasoning to improve robustness across different reasoning patterns. Experiments on datasets across multiple LLMs demonstrate that EVA consistently improves reasoning reliability and achieves strong performance across diverse TableQA settings.

record.abstract_text: The rapid growth of long-form documents presents a fundamental challenge to information retrieval (IR). Their length, dispersed evidence, and complex structures demand approaches that go beyond standard passage-level techniques. This survey provides a comprehensive review of long-document retrieval (LDR) and organizes existing work into three major eras of development. It traces progress from classical lexical and early neural models to pre-trained language models (PLMs) and large language models (LLMs). It highlights core paradigms such as passage aggregation, hierarchical encoding, efficient attention, and LLM-driven re-ranking and retrieval. In addition to methods, the survey summarizes domain-specific applications, available evaluation resources, and the benchmarks that shape empirical study. It identifies open challenges related to efficiency tradeoffs, evidence localization, multimodal alignment, and interpretability. The principal conclusion is that future progress in LDR will depend on hybrid solutions that combine sub-linear indexing, structure-aware modeling, and LLM-based reasoning (resources are available at https://github.com/lmh0921/Long-Document-Retrieval-SURVEY-PLMs-LLMs ).

record.title: Lifecycle Narrative: Reconstructing the Development Process of a Machine Learning Model

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Machine learning models are increasingly proposed for high-risk domains, such as healthcare and public policymaking. However, their growing complexity creates significant obstacles to transparency. This complexity arises from various factors; in this work, we focus on making the organizational development process of a model transparent. A model is often developed over many years and involves multiple version updates, carried out by different individuals, and based on varying subsets of data. To address these issues, we propose a new model reporting framework called a lifecycle narrative, characterized by three dimensions: first, how the purpose of the model has incrementally evolved over time; second, how the data used in the model and the model itself have been developed; and third, what inferences can be made with the model and what the consequences of its use are. We demonstrate these three dimensions using a case study of a high-risk application in healthcare. Our framework complements existing model reporting tools, such as model cards and datasheets, by reconstructing the full lifecycle of the model—a documentation requirement of the EU AI Act. Ultimately, the lifecycle narrative empowers external stakeholders, such as regulators, researchers, citizens, and national competent authorities, to holistically understand a model’s development process.

record.abstract_text: Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT now provide novice programmers with instant, personalized support and are reshaping computing education. While a growing body of work has examined AI's immediate impacts, multi-year classroom evidence remains limited on how students’ awareness of AI, student-AI interaction patterns, and course outcomes evolve as GenAI becomes routine in classrooms. To address this gap, we investigate an introductory Python course across three successive AI-supported cohorts (2023-2025). Using questionnaires, coded student-AI dialogue logs, and course assessment records, we examine cohort-to-cohort shifts in students’ AI awareness, interaction practices, and course outcomes. We find clear cohort-to-cohort differences in students’ relationships with GenAI. Across cohorts, familiarity and prior use became increasingly normalized before course entry, and student-AI interaction shifted from more implementation-oriented use toward more iterative workflows centered on verification, debugging, and refinement. At the same time, course outcomes remained broadly stable. Together, these findings suggest that, during a period in which GenAI became increasingly normalized in everyday life and classrooms, the most visible cohort-level differences appeared in how students sought help, verified their work, and coordinated problem-solving with AI, rather than in final course performance. The central instructional challenge, therefore, is not simply whether students use AI, but how courses can cultivate productive, course-aligned, and agency-preserving forms of AI use.

record.title: Teaching Health Professions Students When Not to Trust Generative AI: A Theory-Informed Framework for Verification-Scaffolded Case-Based Learning

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Background : Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce fluent, context-responsive explanations and clinical suggestions, but the same fluency can conceal factual, evidentiary, or reasoning errors. Health professions students therefore need more than access skills or generic warnings: they need repeated practice deciding when AI advice is warranted, when it requires verification, and when it should be rejected. Aim : To propose a theory-informed, operational framework for teaching appropriate reliance on GenAI through case-based learning. Approach : A focused critical synthesis integrated four bodies of scholarship: GenAI in health professions education, trust and automation bias in human-AI interaction, metacognition and self-regulated learning, and case-based learning. The purpose was conceptual integration rather than exhaustive evidence retrieval or estimation of intervention effects. Framework : Verification-Scaffolded Case-Based Learning (VS-CBL) is a six-phase cycle: Commit, Consult, Challenge, Corroborate, Calibrate, and Consolidate. Students first make and rate an unaided judgment, then consult a documented AI system. They actively test the response for omissions and counterevidence, verify pivotal claims against authoritative sources, decide whether to accept, modify, or reject the advice, and complete an accountable final response plus an unaided transfer task. Faculty prevalidate cases, vary AI accuracy and error subtlety, preserve patient privacy, and scale oversight to clinical risk. Implications : VS-CBL shifts the educational target from AI use or satisfaction to appropriate reliance. It supports measurement of overreliance, underreliance, verification quality, confidence-accuracy calibration, reasoning quality, and delayed independent transfer. The design is adaptable across medicine, nursing, pharmacy, dentistry, rehabilitation, public health, and allied health programmes, including settings with limited connectivity. Conclusion : The educational question is not whether students should trust GenAI in general, but whether trust is warranted for a particular claim, task, and level of risk. VS-CBL offers a testable curriculum architecture for making that judgment visible and teachable. Its effectiveness and implementation burden require prospective, multicentre evaluation.

record.abstract_text: The increasing embrace and utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) within higher education has expressively altered the ways academic knowledge is created, retrieved, and shared. AI-powered tools have become common resources for both students and teachers. The tools generate clear explanations, summarized work, and good-looking content. While these tools provide notable, the growing overdependence upon them has greatly eroded scholarly practices of both students and teachers. The key challenge is the lack of AI content verification practices. In many university settings, the accessibility of AI tools through internet-enabled devices has reduced the need to consult libraries or engage with multiple scholarly sources because users find AI-generated responses so swift, with ready-made content that does not overwork them. The study investigated the growing use of artificial intelligence and the decline of knowledge verification practices among students and teachers in higher education institutions in mid-western Uganda. It explores how AI tools are influencing academic habits, including reduced library engagement, increased reliance on instant digital responses, and the growing perception that information obtained from the internet is fundamentally correct. On the contrary, some content may contain incomplete, misleading, or contextually inappropriate information based on the prompts or instructions given to the system, available training data, or algorithmic limitations. Using a mixed-methods approach involving questionnaires and interviews, the study examined the extent to which students and teachers verify AI-generated content before incorporating it into academic work. The findings of this study highlight the emerging culture of unquestionable trust in AI and its implications for scholarly rigor, critical thinking, and academic integrity in Ugandan universities. The study contributes to ongoing debates on artificial intelligence and digital transformation in higher education in Uganda and globally.

No between-cohort comparison reached significance. A single motivation item declined by one median point in both cohorts. The modal post-encounter preference was a hybrid “solo first, then group” model (7/12, 58%). On the feasibility and acceptability indicators examined, the encounter was delivered as planned in both formats and was rated favorably by learners; these data do not address educational effectiveness. Observed pre-to-post shifts are exploratory and require confirmation in an adequately powered, randomized sample. The provisional instrument is described to support that work.

record.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a tool to support food risk assessment and broader food safety activities in response to the growing complexity of global food supply chains, emerging foodborne hazards, and evolving food fraud practices. Unlike previous reviews that have largely focused on individual AI technologies or specific applications, this review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), transformer-based models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), multimodal learning, and emerging AI paradigms within a unified framework relevant to food risk assessment and food safety decision-making. The review examines their applications in hazard identification, contamination detection, predictive microbiology, risk classification, food fraud detection, surveillance, traceability, and decision-support systems. Particular attention is given to the strengths, limitations, interpretability, validation requirements, and implementation challenges associated with different AI approaches. The integration of AI with multimodal data sources, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, spectroscopy, biosensors, and advanced analytical platforms is also discussed as a means to improve risk prediction, monitoring, and early-warning capabilities. Key challenges include data quality and availability, model generalizability, limited external validation, computational requirements, interpretability, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging developments, including foundation models, federated learning, blockchain, digital twins, edge AI, and multimodal frameworks, are highlighted as promising directions for future research. Overall, this review provides a critical comparative framework for understanding the evolving role of AI in food risk assessment and related food safety applications, while identifying key scientific, technical, and regulatory priorities for future development and implementation. publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background Male infertility contributes to approximately half of all cases of couple infertility worldwide, yet its diagnostic cornerstone, conventional semen analysis anchored in World Health Organization (WHO) criteria, suffers from inter-observer variability that can reach 30–40% for morphological parameters even among trained andrologists. Computer-assisted sperm analysis (CASA) reduced some sources of error but failed to eliminate the subjectivity inherent in morphological classification, particularly for the acrosome, midpiece, and cytoplasmic droplet defect categories. Convolutional neural networks and ensemble deep learning architectures have since demonstrated high classification accuracy on selected benchmark datasets (detailed under Results), prompting fundamental questions about the clinical readiness and translational utility of AI-assisted andrology. Methods (Approach) This is a critical review that synthesises evidence from peer-reviewed studies identified through targeted searches of PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore (through May 2025), covering AI applications in sperm morphology classification, motility analysis, non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) outcome prediction, and sperm selection for intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), supplemented by hand-searching the reference lists of key articles. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for “sperm morphology,” “deep learning,” “convolutional neural network,” “azoospermia,” “testicular sperm extraction,” and “ICSI,” restricted to English-language, peer-reviewed publications. Studies were selected for methodological relevance, recency, and clinical significance rather than through a pre-registered, reproducible systematic protocol; no formal risk-of-bias or quality-appraisal instrument (e.g., QUADAS-2 or PROBAST) was applied. This is a deliberate scope decision, declared here rather than implied: the review is a critical, evidence-synthesising appraisal of a fast-moving field, not a systematic or scoping review, and quantitative performance figures drawn from heterogeneous studies (summarised in Table 1) should be read as illustrative of the state of the field rather than as directly comparable, pooled estimates. Results Deep learning models, including ensemble and attention-augmented convolutional architectures, have reported accuracies of 94% to 96.77% and F1-scores of up to 98.2% for sperm morphology classification, principally on the HuSHeM benchmark dataset; the morphology-classification studies summarised in Table 1 report accuracy, precision, or F1-score rather than AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve). Machine learning models integrating hormonal, genetic, and histopathological features achieve AUC values of 0.807 to above 0.90 for predicting sperm retrieval success in microdissection testicular sperm extraction (m-TESE). For AI-assisted real-time sperm selection during ICSI, a prospective sibling-oocyte study of 646 metaphase II oocytes found only a non-significant trend towards improved fertilisation, whereas a separate, smaller sibling-oocyte comparison, reported to date only as a conference abstract, described a statistically significant improvement in fertilisation; live birth rate data remain scarce. However, the predominance of single-centre, algorithmically homogeneous training datasets, absence of prospective multicentre validation, and the opaque decision logic of most deployed models collectively constrain clinical adoption. Conclusions AI-assisted sperm morphology assessment has attained technical maturity but not clinical readiness. The transition from benchmark accuracy to actionable diagnostic utility requires prospective multicentre validation using clinically diverse and ethnically representative cohorts, live birth rate pre-specified as the primary endpoint, with fertilisation and blastulation rates as secondary endpoints, and the development of explainable AI frameworks compatible with regulatory standards including the EU AI Act. The Middle East and North Africa region, characterised by high rates of male-factor infertility, distinct genetic aetiologies, and constrained laboratory infrastructure, represents both a critical validation environment and an equity-relevant deployment target for these technologies.

record.title: Education After Cognitive Scarcity: A Capability–Experience–Institution Framework for Learning in the Age of Advanced AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Rapid improvements in generative and agentic artificial intelligence are changing a long-standing condition of education: access to high-level cognitive assistance is becoming less scarce. This shift does not make human knowledge obsolete. It changes the design problem. When external systems can explain, synthesize, calculate, generate, critique, plan, translate, code, and increasingly coordinate complex tasks, educators can no longer infer human capability from successful task completion alone. Nor is it sufficient to ask which abilities remain “uniquely human,” because that boundary is technologically unstable and normatively incomplete. This paper proposes a human-development framework for education under cognitive abundance. It introduces Human-Sovereign Capability as a criterion for deciding which capabilities people should remain meaningfully able to exercise even when AI can perform related tasks at higher average performance; Capability Residency as a way to distinguish capability residing in a person, an external system, or a governed human–AI arrangement; and a Learn–Augment–Supervise–Delegate allocation model for deciding the intended relationship between learners and AI. It then extends these decisions into learning design through Productive Friction, a Capability–Experience–Evidence Network, and a Learning Continuity Architecture. The framework culminates in a three-level derivation: Capability → Experience → Institution. The argument is intentionally not that every component concept is new. Cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, automation, scaffolding, tutoring, formative assessment, learner modelling, and lifelong learning have substantial prior literatures. The contribution is an integrated architecture that begins with the normative question of what humans should remain capable of doing, then derives educational experiences, evidence conditions, and institutional obligations from that choice. This paper is presented as an initial framework release from the LiA2036 Research Initiative, with the architecture intended to support inspectable and domain-specific extensions rather than a single universal implementation. The paper closes with research propositions and design questions that can make the framework empirically testable rather than merely rhetorical.

record.abstract_text: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) companions are increasingly used by post-secondary students for emotional support, stress management, and self-management, yet their potential implications for primary care in this population remain unclear. Students may engage with AI companions before encountering purpose-built therapeutic chatbots, which are more often accessed through intentional health-seeking or professional guidance. This distinction may position AI companions as an earlier influence on self-management and subsequent help-seeking. Objective: To examine how artificial intelligence (AI) companions may influence stress regulation, sleep quality, symptom interpretation, and healthcare-seeking behaviour among post-secondary students, and to identify the principal benefits, risks, and unresolved questions relevant to primary care. Methods: A conceptual narrative review was undertaken using literature identified through Harvard University’s Hollis Library and Google Scholar. Evidence related to AI companions, academic stress, sleep quality, emotional support, healthcare-seeking behaviour, primary care, and digital mental health was synthesized using Stress & Coping Theory and the stress-buffering hypothesis as theoretical foundations. Results: AI companions may support stress appraisal, cognitive reframing, emotional reflection, symptom articulation, and self-management before clinical encounters. However, they may also contribute to emotional overreliance, misinformation, reassurance seeking, sleep disruption, and altered help-seeking behaviour. This review proposes conceptual mechanisms linking AI companion engagement with stress regulation, sleep, and pathways into primary care while identifying relational intensity as a clinically meaningful dimension of engagement beyond frequency alone. Conclusion: AI companions should be understood as adjunctive rather than substitutive support. Their clinical relevance is based on how they can shape patients’ experiences before obtaining primary care. Longitudinal research is needed to determine how patterns of engagement influence stress, sleep, and healthcare utilization over time.

record.title: Does Graph Structure Improve AI-Generated Text Detection? A Controlled Audit with Tuned Baselines

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Graph neural network (GNN) detectors of AI-generated text report state-of-the-art accuracy, and the architectural claim that graph topology captures signals invisible to sequential classifiers is now common in the literature. We report the complete lifecycle of one such detector, from construction to falsification. AEGIS, a graph attention network over k-nearest-neighbour text graphs with multi-signal edge weights, reaches 98.50% accuracy on scientific abstracts with only 73K trainable parameters, outperforming five established baselines. We then subject our own system to the evaluation its headline number deserves: generation-time length control, format normalization, leakage-free splits, a tuned frozen-embedding probe as the calibrated null, and a 10 × 10 cross-generator transfer study over three seeds. Under this protocol the graph's apparent contribution collapses from +0.240 AUROC over a surface baseline to −0.0004 AUROC against the tuned probe, inside the measured replication noise floor, and the two detectors' transfer geographies are near-identical (ρ = 0.986). A single untuned regularization default manufactured a +0.027 phantom advantage. The structural differences the graph encodes are real, but they are a re-encoding of information already present in the embeddings. We distil the audit into a practical checklist for evaluating architectural claims in text detection, and argue that accuracy numbers and mechanism claims must be validated separately.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract AI-enabled learning technologies are becoming routine in higher education. However, acceptance research tends to explain adoption through beliefs about technology while paying less attention to the capabilities that learners bring to AI interaction. Although AI literacy has recently been linked to acceptance, it is often modeled as a global score or as separate dimensions, leaving unresolved whether related competencies operate collectively within the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) mechanism. This study tests a higher-order extension of the TAM using survey data from 528 students across three Indonesian universities who had prior experience with AI for learning. AI literacy was specified through awareness, usage skills, critical understanding, and ethics awareness and estimated using a disjoint two-stage partial least squares structural equation modeling procedure. The results support a coherent higher-order representation and show that AI literacy is most strongly associated with perceived ease of use and is also positively related to perceived usefulness and attitude. Within TAM, attitude shows a stronger direct relationship with behavioral intention than usefulness. These findings position AI literacy as a learner capability layer that complements technology beliefs in explaining students’ evaluations of AI-enabled learning technologies. The study contributes a measurement-to-mechanism perspective that maintains practical, critical, and ethical competence in acceptance research and suggests that implementation should consider learner capability alongside access and usability. Because the evidence is cross-sectional, self-reported, and multi-tool, the relationships should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

record.title: AI-Driven Reconstruction of Online Health Narratives Using Agent-Action-Outcome Modeling: Algorithm Development and Validation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background People share health experiences online as stories, not isolated facts. Most computational systems reduce these narratives to keywords or claims, overlooking the agency, causality, and interpretation that determine whether health information is safe or potentially harmful to act on. Content can use medically accurate terminology while describing unsafe behavior, rendering it invisible to fact-checking and keyword approaches. This limitation, which we term narrative blindness , constrains the ability of computational systems to extract, represent, and reason over narratives as coherent wholes. Objective This study introduces the Narrative Builder, a computational framework that reconstructs unstructured online health stories into machine-readable agent-action-outcome (AAO) narrative graphs, preserving structural, causal, and interpretive dimensions. We formalize narrative blindness as a measurable property of natural language processing systems and evaluate whether theory-grounded reconstruction can address it. Methods We operationalized Labov and Waletzky’s sociolinguistic narrative theory within a computational AAO schema, enriched with interpretive dimensions from psychological and clinical communication frameworks. From 5386 Reddit health threads (spanning February 2019 to November 2024), 2 domain experts (a biomedical researcher and a physician) annotated a gold-standard dataset of 2000 segments from 704 threads, with interrater reliability (Krippendorff α) of 0.75 to 0.82 across all annotated tasks (0.78-0.81 for the 4 interpretive classification tasks). A dual-model architecture combining BioBERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations From Transformers for Biomedical Text Mining) with a conditional random field (CRF) layer for AAO extraction and multitask DistilBERT for interpretive classification was evaluated using 5-fold grouped cross-validation, grouped on the annotation-level key to prevent data leakage, with a separate held-out test set and a McNemar test against term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and BioBERT-without-CRF baselines. Results The Narrative Builder achieved a span-level F 1 -score of 0.850 for AAO extraction on the held-out test set, with per-type F 1 of 0.90 (action), 0.83 (agent), and 0.77 (outcome), outperforming the TF-IDF baseline (0.781; P <.001). Labovian stage classification reached macro- F 1 of 0.501, and interpretive dimensions reached macro- F 1 values of 0.466 (emotion), 0.528 (stance), and 0.465 (tone). Clinical-value extraction achieved a precision of 0.90, and Unified Medical Language System concept normalization reached 100% coverage across 12,101 queries. A rule-based causal direction classifier identified 17.3% of segments as candidate outcome-to-action (inverted) patterns, though validation showed limited precision (0.277), and this distribution is reported as exploratory. Single-rater expert review of generated graphs indicated narrative coherence (mean 0.89, SD 0.08) and medical plausibility (mean 0.91, SD 0.07). Conclusions The Narrative Builder reads health stories as coherent wholes rather than isolated facts, producing AAO narrative graphs that retain the agents, actions, outcomes, and emotional framing that determine how individuals interpret and act on health information. By formalizing narrative blindness as a measurable property and reconstructing narrative structure with strong extraction performance, this work establishes narrative reconstruction as a feasible complement to fact-based health informatics, providing structured input for downstream credibility assessment.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background Psychotherapy education increasingly emphasizes technology-assisted methods that extend deliberate practice beyond human supervision. AI has enabled automated skill assessment and patient simulations, yet few studies have examined how students experience such tools in real-world settings alongside established practice modalities. Objective We aimed to evaluate students’ experiences with AI-augmented deliberate practice embedded in an existing psychotherapy course sequence. Secondary aims included identifying implementation barriers, ethical and pedagogical considerations, and factors influencing students’ acceptance of AI-assisted learning. Methods Participants were 29 first-year clinical psychology doctoral students in a 2-quarter psychotherapy sequence at an American Psychological Association–accredited program. In the fall course, students completed weekly peer role-plays and could optionally submit transcripts to CARE for AI feedback to supplement peer feedback. In the winter course, students completed required weekly deliberate practice through Skillsetter video vignettes and could optionally practice with CARE’s voice-based AI-simulated patients, receiving AI and instructor feedback afterward. Surveys with Likert-type and free-response items were voluntary in the fall and required in the winter; 9 and 25 students completed them, respectively. Analyses included descriptive statistics, matched-pairs testing, and thematic analysis. Results In the fall course (n=9), where privacy concerns and survey nonresponse limited data on AI feedback, students rated peer feedback higher than AI feedback on being constructive and helpful (median 3, IQR 3-3 vs median 2, IQR 2-2; P =.02) and recognizing areas to improve (mean 5.22, SD 0.83 vs mean 4.33, SD 0.87; P =.046), citing transcription errors and a narrow focus on empathy while valuing AI’s alternative phrasing. In the winter course (n=25), Skillsetter was rated higher than CARE only for learning from mistakes (mean 4.52, SD 2.00 vs mean 3.20, SD 2.04; P =.03); immersion, spontaneous responding, communication beyond words, and alliance building did not differ significantly. Students valued CARE for interactive practice not possible with vignettes but reported undetected vocal pauses (20/25, 80%), insufficient realism (14/25, 56%), and limited emotional expression (13/25, 52%), and raised concerns about AI replacing peer support (22/25, 88%) and peer interaction (20/25, 80%). Asked about AI broadly, students expressed mixed views, citing concerns about supplanted relational dynamics, nonconsensual data use, and generative AI’s environmental impacts. Conclusions Embedding AI-augmented deliberate practice into an existing course sequence was feasible, but students’ experiences favored established methods: they preferred human over AI feedback and described video vignettes as more realistic than voice-based AI interactions, while valuing AI-simulated patients for interactive practice other modalities could not provide. Implementation barriers included feedback quality, transcription accuracy, and instructor time required to supplement AI feedback. Perceptions of AI’s instructional utility appeared contingent on students’ trust in the technology, suggesting future deployments should weigh a sample’s attitudes toward AI and its value relative to existing training resources.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background Natural language processing and AI models are increasingly used to extract emotional signals from textual data; however, systematic validation of different computational paradigms in emotionally complex relational contexts remains limited. Such approaches may contribute to digital health research, particularly in the fields of digital mental health and couples therapy, where understanding emotional expressions within romantic relationships is especially relevant. Objective This study aimed to compare a lexicon-based approach (NRC Emotion Lexicon) and a transformer-based model (Pysentimiento) in detecting affective patterns within spontaneous romantic relationship narratives and to evaluate their criterion-related associations with a theory-driven measure of relational well-being. Methods In this cross-sectional exploratory study, 112 Spanish adults completed the Couple Flourishing Measure (CFM) and provided an open-ended description of their romantic relationship. Narratives were analyzed using both computational approaches to generate emotion and sentiment indices. Pearson correlations were computed between model outputs and CFM scores. Steiger Z tests were conducted to compare dependent correlations across models. Results Both approaches showed significant associations with couple flourishing, although the transformer-based model yielded stronger correlations for several affective dimensions, particularly positive sentiment ( r =0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.76) and negative sentiment ( r =−0.74, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.65). The lexicon-based approach showed smaller associations, primarily for negative emotions. Steiger Z tests identified significant between-model differences for disgust ( P =.04), joy ( P =.01), sadness ( P =.004), surprise ( P =.03), and positive and negative sentiment (both P <.001), but not for anger or fear. Conclusions In this sample, Pysentimiento showed stronger associations with couple flourishing than the NRC Emotion Lexicon across several affective dimensions, although differences were not consistent across all categories. These findings support the value of theory-driven external criteria for evaluating computational emotion detection in relational narratives and underscore the importance of context-sensitive interpretation when applying AI tools in psychologically sensitive domains. These findings also highlight the potential relevance of computational emotion analysis for digital health research, particularly in digital mental health and couples therapy research, although further validation in clinical settings is needed before clinical implementation.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background AI is increasingly embedded in health care and digital health applications, shaping clinical processes as well as how patients access information and participate in care. Research on bias in medical AI has largely focused on technical and performance-related disparities. Less attention has been paid to how such biases may affect patients’ access, understanding, trust, and opportunities for meaningful involvement in care. Objective This scoping review aimed to map how studies of bias in medical AI describe patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment and the digital divide and to identify gaps across technical, social, structural, and patient-centered perspectives. Methods This scoping review followed JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute) methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost databases were searched in August 2025 and supplemented by Google Scholar searches. Peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 onward were included if they addressed bias in medical AI and described patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment or digital inequality. Data charting focused on AI application types, bias dimensions, patient empowerment domains, digital divide–related factors, intersectionality, and debiasing strategies. Findings were synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results The search identified 497 records, of which 22 studies met the inclusion criteria. Bias was represented as a multidimensional sociotechnical phenomenon, with social bias identified most frequently (21/22 studies), followed by algorithmic bias (16/22 studies), structural bias (14/22 studies), and design-related bias (12/22 studies). Patient empowerment was most frequently addressed through involvement in care (n=13), followed by health literacy (n=9) and trust and assurance (n=7), whereas broader psychosocial and everyday-life domains were addressed less frequently. Digital divide–related factors were identified in 19 of the 22 studies, with digital literacy and usability barriers reported most frequently. Seven studies considered 2 or more social or structural dimensions of disadvantage. Although many studies discussed approaches that could mitigate bias-related barriers, explicit empirical evaluation of debiasing strategies in relation to patient empowerment or digital equity was largely absent. Conclusions Patient-related consequences of bias in medical AI extend beyond algorithmic performance and are reflected in access, understanding, trust, and involvement in care. Broader empowerment dimensions, multidimensional disadvantage, and empirically evaluated mitigation strategies remain comparatively underexplored.

record.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. Written from the perspective of a primary school teacher and principal, this perspective paper examines three interrelated concerns of the author herself. These concerns arose from a wish to protect her pupils and led her to study the topic for her own professional development and to help her colleagues make teaching safer and better. They concern developing critical thinking towards AI-generated answers, protecting the personal data of minors, and the fear that excessive assistance from AI will weaken pupils' thinking. Drawing on a narrative, non-systematic review of recent research on cognitive offloading, the European and Greek regulatory framework, and illustrative examples from the author's own teaching practice and lesson scenarios for primary school, it argues that the fear of cognitive dependence is a plausible concern rather than an established finding for primary school pupils. The available evidence, which comes mainly from adolescents and adults, suggests that the form of AI support (whether it replaces the learner's effort or scaffolds it) may be an important factor. AI is regarded throughout as a valuable tool; the risk lies mainly in the way it is used.
