record.abstract_text: The Research Topic begins with Achuthan's Artificial intelligence and learner autonomy: a meta-analysis of self-regulated and self-directed learning, which provides a broad empirical examination of the relationship between AI and learner autonomy. Synthesizing 32 empirical studies, 92 effect sizes, and 3,029 participants, the study examines the effects of AI-based interventions on SRL, self-directed learning (SDL), different dimensions and phases of SRL, and learning outcomes. The findings indicate positive effects of AI interventions on overall SRL and SDL, with particularly notable effects during the forethought phase, including goal setting and planning. At the same time, less consistent effects for behavioral regulation point to an important design challenge: supporting learners in knowing what to do and why to do it does not necessarily ensure that they will translate those intentions into effective action. The findings therefore provide encouraging evidence for AI as a scaffold for self-regulation while highlighting the importance of designing support across the full SRL cycle.Building on this macro-level evidence, Agustin's AI as a co-regulator: relational design for strengthening self-regulated learning addresses the theoretical mechanics of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in Winne and Hadwin's COPES architecture, this conceptual paper tackles a core dilemma in educational technology: how can AI assist learners without eroding the cognitive agency and productive struggle essential to self-regulation? Agustin introduces "productive metacognitive friction" -the deliberate structuring of challenge and discrepancy within AI interaction -as a design mechanism to prevent passive reliance. The article presents five relational design principles alongside an evaluation framework prioritizing learner autonomy, interpretability, process integrity, and long-term developmental growth across both formal education and workplace reskilling environments.Moving from meta-analytic synthesis and conceptual frameworks to empirical classroom research, Gu et al.'s Fostering feedback literacy by scaffolding self-regulated feedback: a comparative study of GenAI and human peers examines the operational mechanisms through which GenAI fosters feedback literacya key component of self-regulated learning. In a comparative mixed-methods study of first-year undergraduates in Hong Kong, the authors compare the developmental impact of GenAI-generated feedback against traditional human peer review. Their findings demonstrate that GenAI yields a statistically significant improvement in feedback literacy over human peer feedback alone. Qualitative evidence reveals that this advantage stems from GenAI's ability to scaffold distinct self-regulatory behaviors: providing immediate, non-judgmental spaces for goal setting, structured planning, critical evaluation, and real-time self-reflection. By removing the interpersonal friction and psychological safety concerns common in peer review, GenAI emerges as an effective tool for cultivating student feedback literacy.Finally, Chang et al.'s "Should I tell my teacher?" Student AI disclosure practices, stigma, and selfregulated learning in higher education examines the affective, social, and institutional factors that influence how learners adopt these tools in practice. Focusing on undergraduate students at a Canadian university, the authors explore the intersection of student AI disclosure practices, social stigma, and SRL processes. Their findings illuminate a key tension: while transparent disclosure to instructors correlates with proactive self-regulated learning behaviors (a "transparent-disclosure pattern"), fear of academic judgment and social stigmatization often triggers an "anxious-concealment pattern." Highly anxious students who use AI heavily are more likely to conceal their usage or restrict sharing to peer networks. This study highlights that technical scaffolds cannot succeed in a vacuum; institutional policies and pedagogical environments must account for emotional and social dynamics to prevent secrecy from undermining reflective SRL practices.Considered together, the four articles in this Research Topic illustrate that AI's role in self-regulated learning extends far beyond simple automation or content delivery. Achuthan's meta-analysis provides evidence of AI's potential to strengthen SRL and SDL, while also identifying limitations in behavioral regulation. Agustin's framework addresses this challenge conceptually by positioning AI as a co-regulator that supports learners without displacing their agency. Gu et al. demonstrate how such support can be enacted in feedback processes, whereas Chang et al. show how emotions, stigma, and institutional expectations shape learners' decisions about AI use. This collection highlights that realizing the promise of AI-supported self-regulated learning requires more than personalization or automation. Research and design must examine how AI can scaffold regulatory processes, support learner autonomy and human agency, and safeguard against cognitive over-reliance.

record.abstract_text: This study set out to examine how artificial intelligence is currently being employed in Jordanian government academic libraries, and to look closely at the ethical questions that come with that employment, particularly around three areas: the contribution of artificial intelligence to developing library services, the extent of commitment to information ethics and privacy, and the institutional and technical obstacles standing in the way of wider adoption. The descriptive-analytical approach was adopted for this purpose. A questionnaire covering these three areas was built and distributed to a random sample of (137) employees drawn from a total population of (258) employees across Jordanian government academic libraries, a sample that made up (53.1%) of the population. Results indicated that the role artificial intelligence currently plays in improving library services is still moderate (mean=3.154), and that commitment to information ethics and privacy likewise falls at a moderate level (mean=3.318), with legal accountability and intellectual-property protection drawing somewhat more attention than transparency and algorithmic neutrality. The challenges axis came out highest of the three (mean=3.638), driven mainly by staff resistance to new technologies and unease over a shrinking human role in decision-making. None of the differences across gender, age group, educational level, or years of experience reached statistical significance, suggesting these perceptions are broadly shared across staff regardless of their personal or professional background. In light of these results, the study recommends that library administrations put in place a clear code of ethics for artificial-intelligence use, invest in dedicated staff training, and move forward through small pilot projects before any large-scale rollout, while urging the Ministry of Higher Education to issue a unified national framework for artificial-intelligence ethics across academic institutions.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Corporate ESG disclosure has shifted toward narrative form, yet vendor ESG ratings that most empirical work depends on show substantial disagreement across providers, and encoders dominant in financial text analysis inherit a 512-token ceiling that discards most of a typical 10-K. HET-ESGFormer combines hierarchical long-document encoding, heterogeneity-aware sparse expert routing conditioned on industry sector and firm size, and a dual-channel explanation layer subject to faithfulness verification. The framework is evaluated on 3,182 U.S.-listed firms over 2015 to 2024 using 10-K filings, sustainability reports, earnings call transcripts, and ESG-tagged news. Against nine baselines spanning econometric, dictionary-based, contextual encoder, sparse-attention, and time-series approaches, HET-ESGFormer reduces return RMSE from 0.0417 to 0.0389 and QLIKE from 0.148 to 0.128, with Diebold-Mariano tests rejecting equal predictive accuracy against every baseline after correction for multiple comparisons. The text channel's marginal contribution to downside risk prediction is materially larger than its contribution to return prediction, widening at longer forecast horizons, indicating that ESG narratives carry more information about risk than about expected return. Ablations reveal a decoupling between predictive skill and explanation faithfulness: removing the consistency regularizer barely affects accuracy but sharply degrades explanation quality. The dual-channel explanation improves ERASER comprehensiveness by 50% over SHAP applied to XGBoost, and human raters significantly prefer the framework's rationales over SHAP-based rationales on trustworthiness. Decile-sorted long-short portfolios deliver a post-cost Sharpe ratio of 1.31 against 0.74 and 0.62 for portfolios built on Refinitiv and MSCI ratings, and pass VaR backtests at 95% coverage. The results support text-based ESG modeling as an alternative to vendor-rating-based approaches, particularly where downside risk management and traceable explanation are jointly required.

record.abstract_text: Autonomous systems pose liability issues when automated decisions contribute to harm, failure, or non-compliance with regulations. This research paper proposes a decision-support model for categorizing liability cues under European Union and Indian law. The source datasets were MultiEURLEX and IndicLegalQA, and a rule-based proxy mapping was developed to assign five labels: damage, defect, liability, regulation, and risk. This model is based on word-level and character-level TF-IDF, jurisdiction encoding, and a One-vs-Rest Linear Support Vector Machine classifier for multi-label classification. record.abstract_text: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) demands urgent empirical investigation into its role in undergraduate studies. This study examines the transformative impact of these tools in higher education (HE) in Algeria. The primary objective is to investigate how students at the National School of Computer Science (ESI) in Algiers use GenAI tools. The research also aims to provide evidence-based recommendations for Algerian HE institutions on academic integrity and pedagogical adaptation. Using a case study methodology, the research combined a GenAI use survey of 74 students with an educational experiment involving 12 teams in November 2023. The findings reveal a high adoption rate: 94.44% of students use GenAI, and 73.61% report daily use. GenAI serves as a powerful ancillary educational tool that shifts focus from content memorisation to competency application. In the experimental phase, 100% of teams relied on GenAI tools to execute the core cognitive and text-generation tasks. However, several groups integrated conventional auxiliary software to support their final visual deliverables. However, the quality of interaction remains narrow. Practical implications for HE institutions in Algeria suggest that teachers and trainers must restructure tutorials and practical work to favour complex, collaborative problem-solving. Additionally, institutions should prioritise formative over summative assessment and implement comprehensive AI literacy training to safeguard academic integrity.

record.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming manufacturing supply chains by enabling intelligent decision-making, adaptive operations, and more efficient resource utilization. Its potential to advance sustainable operations management, however, extends beyond technological adoption to the organizational integration of AI capabilities into operational processes and sustainability-oriented strategies. Despite growing scholarly attention, research in this field remains fragmented across technological applications, manufacturing functions, organizational conditions, and sustainability dimensions. In particular, limited conceptual integration exists regarding how AI capabilities are translated into operational transformation and under what organizational and technological conditions such transformation generates sustainable value. To address these limitations, this study conducts a systematic literature review and structured research gap analysis of peer-reviewed studies published between 2016 and 1 June 2026. The review examines the intellectual evolution of the field, synthesizes dominant research themes, evaluates AI applications across manufacturing and supply chain operations, and critically assesses their implications for operational, environmental, economic, and social sustainability. The synthesis highlights an emerging shift from isolated, function-specific AI applications towards interconnected and increasingly autonomous operational ecosystems, supported by the convergence of AI with the Internet of Things (IoT), digital twins, cyber-physical systems, and advanced analytics. These developments create opportunities for predictive and prescriptive decision-making, intelligent production planning, predictive maintenance, quality optimization, resource efficiency, supply chain visibility, and disruption management. Nevertheless, the realization of these benefits remains contingent upon organizational readiness, digital infrastructure maturity, data quality, workforce capabilities, effective governance, and the alignment of technological investments with sustainability priorities. The review further identifies persistent theoretical, methodological, technological, organizational, and empirical gaps, particularly concerning human–AI collaboration, implementation scalability, algorithmic accountability, sustainability trade-offs, and the assessment of long-term performance outcomes. Building on these insights, the study develops an AI-Driven Sustainable Operations Management Strategic Framework that integrates AI technological capabilities, organizational and digital enablers, AI-enabled operational transformation mechanisms, sustainability-oriented governance, and multidimensional performance outcomes. By connecting technological potential with organizational transformation and sustainability performance, the proposed framework provides an integrative conceptual foundation for understanding AI-enabled sustainable value creation across manufacturing supply chains. It also establishes a structured agenda for future research and offers strategic implications for manufacturing organizations and policymakers seeking to advance responsible AI adoption, strengthen operational resilience, and achieve sustainable long-term competitiveness.

record.venue: Journal of Education and Learning Reviews
record.abstract_text: Background and Aim: Evidence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary science education remains limited. This systematic review examined students’ conceptual understanding and engagement, teachers’ pedagogical strategies and challenges, and students’ critical thinking and scientific inquiry. Materials and Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, ERIC, Scopus, and Lens.org were searched for peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026. Two authors independently screened 187 unique records (Cohen’s κ = .78), identifying 20 eligible studies. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Framework synthesis integrated findings, informed by Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK). Results: Seven studies assessed AI capabilities rather than classroom implementation. Only two compared learning outcomes across conditions; none employed a randomized controlled design. Student perceptions and engagement were generally positive, whereas learning outcomes were mixed. A chatbot supporting self-regulated learning outperformed a rule-based chatbot, but ChatGPT-4o yielded smaller gains than peer collaboration. Teachers reported concerns regarding content accuracy, assessment reliability, and instructional readiness. Generative AI matched or exceeded student performance on structured examinations but demonstrated lower grading reliability than human assessors. Evidence concerning critical thinking was particularly limited. Richer reasoning was reported with dialogue-oriented tools or teacher guidance, whereas answer-seeking use of general-purpose tools was associated with weaker reasoning. Conclusion: Pedagogical structuring was recurrently associated with productive AI use, although causal inference remains limited. A provisional model warrants empirical testing. Priorities include structured tasks, science-specific teacher development, human assessment oversight, explicit AI literacy instruction, school governance, and controlled comparisons of structured and unstructured use across secondary science classrooms.

record.abstract_text: With the growing adoption of generative AI (GenAI) in higher education, concerns have emerged about excessive AI dependence and the inappropriate use of AI-generated content. However, few studies have examined the relationships among AI dependency (AID), cognitive offloading (CO), and AI-giarism (AIG). This study examined the direct and indirect associations among these constructs among 191 preservice physics teachers (PSPTs) from universities in Sulawesi, Indonesia, using a quantitative cross-sectional design and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results showed that AID was positively associated with CO (β = 0.664, p < 0.001) and AIG (β = 0.603, p < 0.001), while CO was positively associated with AIG (β = 0.242, p = 0.003). CO also showed a statistically significant indirect association between AID and AIG (β = 0.160, p = 0.003). The model accounted for 44.0% of the variance in CO and 61.6% of the variance in AIG. These findings indicate that AID is associated with self-reported AIG both directly and indirectly through CO within the specified model. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish causal relationships, and the self-reported outcome does not confirm actual incidents of academic misconduct. These findings highlight the importance of teacher education approaches that promote responsible AI use, independent reasoning, critical evaluation of AI-generated information, and transparent disclosure of AI assistance.

As health insurers adopt AI-enabled automation, these challenges become more complex if decisions are not explainable, evidence-based, auditable, and supported by human oversight. This study introduces a secure AI-driven decision-support framework for prior authorization that integrates explainable decision logic, policy-rule traceability, clinical-evidence mapping, bias monitoring, human review checkpoints, and appeal-ready explanations within a single governance model. record.abstract_text: The study aimed to check the association of ChatGPT use and critical thinking on academic integrity. The research design is cross-sectional correlational study to collect data from university students aged from 18 to 23 years old. The sample size was 600 students taken via purposive sampling from the University of Gujrat, Pakistan. Standardized psychological scales of ChatGPT usage scale, critical thinking evaluation scale, and academic integrity scales were used. Our findings showed that ChatGPT has no significant effect on academic integrity but has positive effect on critical thinking. While critical thinking has positive effect on academic integrity. It showed that ChatGPT doesn’t directly change cheating behavior, but it can boost critical thinking for students, and that improved critical thinking is what increases academic integrity. Implications of the findings are discussed.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as an important driver of workplace transformation, influencing how organisations organise work, make decisions, monitor employees, develop skills and deliver services. Unlike earlier forms of workplace automation that primarily focused on replacing manual or repetitive tasks, contemporary AI systems can analyse large volumes of data, support managerial decisions, predict operational outcomes, monitor performance and interact with employees and customers. The study examines the relationships between Artificial Intelligence-Driven Workplace Transformation and Employee Voice in the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry. The study adopted a cross-sectional survey in its investigation of the variables. The primary source of data was generated through a structured questionnaire. The population of the study was 4,700 employees from 17 selected Oil and Gas companies in Rivers State, Nigeria. The sample size was determined using the Taro Yamane formula at a 5% precision, and the result was 369. Therefore, the study respondents were made up of 369 employees from the oil and gas industry. Artificial Intelligence-Driven workplace Transformation was used as a predictor variable, while Employee Voice was measured with employee participation in decision-making, Upward Communication and expression of Concerns. The validity was confirmed by academic experts, and reliability was confirmed using Cronbach’s Alpha coefficients above 0.70. The hypotheses were tested using Spearman’s Rank Order Correlation Statistics. The tests were carried out at a 0.05 significance level. Findings from the study revealed that there is a significant relationship between Artificial Intelligence-Driven Workplace Transformation and Employee Voice in the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry. The study concludes that Artificial Intelligence-Driven Workplace Transformation significantly influence Employee Voice in the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry. The study recommends that oil and gas companies should establish structured mechanisms that allow employees to participate meaningfully in decisions concerning the introduction and implementation of artificial intelligence technologies.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) writing companions are changing how second-language (L2) writers plan, formulate, and revise texts. Yet improved textual fluency does not necessarily indicate deeper learning or stronger independent writing ability. This conceptual article develops a framework for interpreting AI-assisted L2 writing through the Cognitive Process Model of Writing, Cognitive Load Theory, and the Output Hypothesis. It argues that AI assistance may redistribute rather than simply reduce cognitive effort: linguistic suggestions can ease some local formulation demands, while evaluating, adapting, and verifying generated language creates additional monitoring demands. Whether this redistribution supports learning depends on the learner’s agency, the transparency of the task, and the instructional design. The article proposes a three-phase pedagogical model: supported conceptual ideation, autonomous drafting, and collaborative critical revision. Across these phases, AI support is deliberately varied so that learners can benefit from assistance without surrendering authorship, monitoring, or opportunities for linguistic retrieval. The paper is conceptual and does not report an empirical experiment. It therefore offers propositions and a research agenda rather than claims of measured effects. The framework can guide future classroom research, instrument development, and responsible integration of generative AI into L2 writing curricula.

record.title: Transforming Science Education through Artificial Intelligence (AI): Opportunities, Challenges, and Implications for Students' Critical Thinking Skills in the Digital Era.
record.venue: Assoeltan Indonesian Journal of Community Research and Engagement

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping science education by expanding access to information, supporting adaptive instruction, enabling simulations, and providing timely feedback. This article examines the opportunities, challenges, and implications of AI integration for students’ critical thinking in the digital era. Using a narrative literature review, the study synthesizes foundational scholarship on AI in education, science learning, AI literacy, and critical thinking, alongside recent reviews and international guidance. The synthesis indicates that AI can support critical thinking when it is embedded in inquiry-oriented activities that require students to formulate questions, interpret scientific evidence, compare explanations, identify limitations, and justify conclusions. AI-supported simulations, conversational systems, and feedback tools may make abstract concepts more accessible and provide opportunities for iterative reasoning. However, these benefits are not automatic. Hallucinated information, algorithmic bias, privacy risks, unequal access, academic integrity concerns, and cognitive over-reliance may weaken learning if AI outputs are accepted without verification. The article argues that AI should function as a cognitive partner rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual work. Effective integration therefore requires scientific and AI literacy, teacher mediation, transparent assessment, ethical safeguards, and learning tasks that make reasoning visible. A human-centred approach can help science education use AI to strengthen, rather than displace, independent and evidence-based thinking.

record.title: Do AI Symptom Checkers Help or Hinder Timely Care-Seeking for Early Heart Disease? A Narrative Review of the Evidence by Insurance Status

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Cardiovascular disease killed 919,032 people in the United States in 2023, and how long people wait before getting help shapes much of that toll. The wait is not the same for everyone. In a 24-hospital U.S. registry, 48.6% of uninsured heart attack patients waited more than six hours, compared with 44.6% of insured patients who worried about costs and 39.3% of insured patients who did not. AI symptom checkers now show up at exactly the moment people decide whether to get care. Yet I found no study that measures whether using one changes how fast people seek care for heart symptoms, or whether the answer depends on insurance. This narrative review, organized with guidance from PRISMA 2020, pulls together evidence on four things: how accurate symptom checkers are, how they change people's plans for care, who uses them, and how insurance shapes the decision to seek cardiac care. I searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar between June and September 2026, along with publisher, journal, and government websites, and checked the reference lists of key studies. Twenty-two sources form the core evidence base: 20 peer-reviewed studies and 2 survey reports that were not peer-reviewed. Because the studies ranged from simulated-case audits to national registries, I appraised each one with four questions (real patients or simulated cases, observed behavior or stated intention, independence from the tool's developer, and how representative the sample was) and synthesized the findings narratively. Following the Commonwealth Fund, I treated insurance as three levels: adequately insured, underinsured, and uninsured. The evidence cuts both ways. Symptom checkers reduce uncertainty and usually catch emergencies. But in the largest real-world dataset, users lowered the urgency of their care plans eight times as often as they raised it. Most tools triage no better than an average layperson, and in studies with real patients, 2-9% of cases were under-triaged. In a randomized trial, people using AI chatbots made no better care decisions than people using other sources. The typical user is insured, college-educated, and female, so little is known about the groups most likely to delay. I argue that insurance likely decides whether a symptom checker speeds care up or slows it down. Insured users can act on advice, or double-check it, at little cost. Uninsured and underinsured users are the least able to catch a falsely reassuring answer. Three hypotheses follow. Among adequately insured adults, prior symptom checker use will shorten the time to professional consultation for early cardiac symptoms. Among uninsured adults, it will not shorten that time and may lengthen it. Underinsured adults will fall in between, and pairing advice with navigation to low-cost care should narrow the gaps among the three groups. I outline an equity-focused design with measurable safety thresholds, such as sensitivity for emergencies of 95% or higher and harmful under-triage in 2% or fewer encounters, along with community health worker review and community governance. I also propose four studies to test the hypotheses: an audit of standardized cardiac cases, a prospective cohort stratified by insurance tier, a stepped-wedge trial of community health worker navigation, and qualitative interviews.

record.title: Neural Mechanisms of Willed Attention Control

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Cueing paradigms are commonly used to study the neural mechanisms of visual spatial attention control. In these paradigms, each trial starts with an external cue, which instructs the subject to pay covert attention to a spatial location in anticipation of an impending stimulus (instructed attention). Recent work has introduced a new type of cue which prompts the subject to spontaneously decide which spatial location to attend (willed attention). We studied the neural mechanisms of willed attention control by analyzing fMRI and EEG data recorded at two institutions (UF and UC Davis) using the same willed attention paradigm. The findings include: (1) both instructional cues and the choice cue activated the DAN, (2) the choice cue additionally activated a frontoparietal decision network consisting of dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), anterior insula (AI), anterior prefrontal cortex (APFC), dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), and inferior parietal lobule (IPL), (3) the decision about where to attend can be decoded in frontoparietal decision network in choice trials but not in instructional trials, and (4) EEG alpha oscillation patterns immediately preceding the choice cue, but not the instructional cues, predicted the postcue direction of attention and the frontoparietal decision network activity. Based on these findings we proposed a model of willed attention control suggesting how the direction of visual spatial attention was decided upon in the absence of external instructions.
